newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus KEO keeps expansion options open.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus KEO keeps expansion options open.

text.p: Cyprus beer and wine manufacturer KEO on Thursday said it was keeping its options open for expanding into other sectors of the refreshments industry.
The 70-year old company, one of Cyprus's largest industrial plants, is active in the canning and fruit juice sectors along with its wines and trademark beer.

"We are having thoughts and we have some ideas regarding the seasonality of our products, and the fact that they are exposed somewhat depending on tourist arrivals and on climatological conditions," company chairman Elias Pantelides told a news conference.
KEO has not disclosed what fields it could expand in, but last year the company made a failed bid to purchase a local company which has the Cyprus licence to bottle soft drinks Pepsi, 7-Up and Ivi.
The group posted pre-tax profits of 343,000 pounds ($650,000) in 1996, on sales of 31.4 million pounds, compared to pre-tax profits of 568,000 pounds on sales of 29.8 million in 1995.
It expects 1997 results to be slightly better, although market trends appear to be on the same level as 1996, managing director Akis Zambartas said.

"Generally speaking beer sales locally, of all the brands on the Cyprus market, were down by 5.86 percent in 1996 and between January and June (this year) they were down by an additional five percent," said Zambartas, quoting official statistics.
But Zambartas said the company's debut in the bottled water market with its Ayios Nicolaos brand in 1995 was an outstanding success, and KEO beer sales in the Greek islands were very encouraging.
"We are now leaders in the bottled water market," he said.

The group has blamed high labour costs, an increase in the cost of grape purchases because of a protracted drought affecting the island and a redundancy scheme enacted for members of staff in a subsidiary for the decline in 1996 profits.
In addition to 1996 taxation of 386,000 pounds, the company has made provision for further tax of 855,000 pounds based on an inland revenue department decision in late 1996.

Inland revenue had rejected KEO's calculation of taxes on profits and losses of companies within the group on a group relief basis between 1990 and 1995. The issue is now being studied by company lawyers, Pantelides said.
Zambartas said the company was concentrating on producing higher quality bottled wines and to diversify from indigenous grape varieties, many of which are for the mass-production of wine.

The company, he said, has created vineyards with indigenous and imported grape varieties. "We have adopted modern methods taking into account the balances of the ecosystem... We want to develop the fame of Cyprus wines," said Zambartas. ($=0.527 Cyprus pounds)
